acton: Acton sits about 21 miles west-northwest of Boston along Route 2, west of Concord, bordering Westford, Littleton, Carlisle, Stow, Maynard, Sudbury and Boxborough.
arlington: Arlington is a Middlesex County town about six miles northwest of Boston.
ashland: Ashland is a Middlesex County town in the MetroWest region.
auburn: Auburn is a Worcester County town bordering the city of Worcester.
ayer: Incorporated in 1871 from part of Groton, Ayer grew as a major railroad junction and sits beside the former Fort Devens.
bedford: Bedford is a Middlesex County suburb about 21 miles northwest of Boston.
bellingham: Bellingham sits on the southwestern edge of Greater Boston along the Interstate 495 corridor, and is also part of the Providence metropolitan area.
belmont: Belmont is a western suburb of Boston in Middlesex County whose population grew more than 10% between 2010 and 2020.
beverly: Beverly is a North Shore city that includes the neighborhoods of Ryal Side, North Beverly, Centerville, Cove, Montserrat, Beverly Farms and Prides Crossing.
braintree: Braintree is a Norfolk County community south of Boston with access to the MBTA Red Line.
brookline: Brookline borders six Boston neighborhoods and the city of Newton, and is known as the birthplace of President John F. Kennedy.
burlington: Burlington is a Middlesex County town north of Boston.
cambridge: Cambridge sits directly across the Charles River from Boston and is the most populous city in Middlesex County.
canton: Canton is a Norfolk County town about 15 miles southwest of downtown Boston.
chelmsford: Chelmsford was incorporated in 1655 and its early economy was built on lumber mills, limestone quarries and kilns.
concord: Concord was established in 1635 as one of the first inland settlements of the colony, near where the Sudbury and Assabet rivers form the Concord River.
danvers: Danvers, originally known as Salem Village, sits on the Danvers River near the northeastern coast of Massachusetts.
dedham: Dedham, the Norfolk County seat on Boston's southwestern border, is home to the Fairbanks House, the oldest surviving timber-frame house in the United States.
douglas: Douglas is a southern Worcester County town that includes the Douglas State Forest.
dover: Dover is a residential town on the south bank of the Charles River, where almost all residential zoning requires lots of one acre or more.
fitchburg: Fitchburg is the third-largest city in Worcester County and home to Fitchburg State University.
framingham: Incorporated in 1700, Framingham is the largest municipality in MetroWest, covering about 25 square miles.
franklin: Franklin is a Norfolk County community and home to the first public library in the country, the Franklin Public Library.
grafton: Grafton includes North Grafton, Grafton and South Grafton, and is home to the Hassanamisco Reservation and the Willard House and Clock Museum.
groton: Groton is a northwestern Middlesex County town roughly 45 miles from Boston.
holden: Holden was founded in 1741 and includes the village of Jefferson.
holliston: Holliston is the only town in Middlesex County that borders both Norfolk and Worcester counties.
hopedale: Hopedale began as a Christian utopian community and was later home to the Draper Corporation loom works until 1980.
hopkinton: Hopkinton is the starting point of the Boston Marathon, held every April on Patriots' Day.
hudson: Before becoming a town in 1866, Hudson was a village of Marlborough known as Feltonville, and it was a shoe-manufacturing mill town for over a century.
leicester: Leicester is a Worcester County town west of Worcester.
leominster: Leominster is the second-most populous city in Worcester County, crossed by Route 2 and Route 12.
lexington: Lexington is the site of the first shots of the American Revolutionary War, fought on April 19, 1775.
littleton: Littleton is a Middlesex County town that includes Littleton Common.
lunenburg: Lunenburg is a north Worcester County town.
marlborough: Marlborough became a prosperous industrial town in the 19th century and shifted to high-technology industry after the Massachusetts Turnpike was built.
medfield: Medfield is about 17 miles southwest of Boston and is home to Hinkley Pond and the historic Peak House.
medway: Medway is a Norfolk County town southwest of Boston.
mendon: Mendon is part of the Blackstone River Valley National Heritage Corridor and celebrated its 350th anniversary in 2017.
milford: Milford, settled in 1662, grew into an industrial and granite-quarrying community in the 19th century near the source of the Charles River.
millbury: Millbury is a Blackstone Valley town just south of Worcester.
millis: Millis is about 19 miles southwest of downtown Boston, bordered by Norfolk, Sherborn, Holliston, Medfield and Medway.
milton: Milton lies between the Neponset River and the Blue Hills, directly south of Boston's Dorchester and Mattapan neighborhoods.
natick: Natick sits near the center of the MetroWest region, about ten miles west of Boston, and was the state's center of population in the 2000 to 2020 censuses.
needham: Needham is home to Olin College of Engineering and four commuter rail stations on the Needham Line.
newton: Newton is made up of thirteen villages about eight miles west of downtown Boston.
northborough: Northborough, also spelled Northboro, is a Worcester County town east of Worcester.
northbridge: Northbridge, whose town hall is in the village of Whitinsville, is part of the Blackstone River Valley National Heritage Corridor.
norwood: Norwood sits on the Neponset River in Norfolk County and is part of Greater Boston.
paxton: Paxton is a small Worcester County town northwest of Worcester.
peabody: Peabody is a North Shore city known for its industrial history.
princeton: Princeton is home to the main entrance of Wachusett Mountain, which straddles its border with Westminster.
quincy: Quincy, the City of Presidents, is the birthplace of John Adams and John Quincy Adams and the largest city in Norfolk County.
randolph: Randolph is a Norfolk County community that adopted a council-manager form of government in 2010.
reading: Reading is a Middlesex County town about 16 miles north of central Boston.
rutland: Rutland is the geographic center of Massachusetts, marked by the Central Tree on Central Tree Road.
salem: Salem is a historic coastal city on the North Shore and was one of the most significant seaports in early American history.
sherborn: Sherborn is a MetroWest town that shares its public school system with Dover.
shirley: Shirley, about thirty miles west-northwest of Boston, has a well-preserved historic New England town center.
shrewsbury: Shrewsbury, incorporated in 1727, grew alongside Worcester and Lake Quinsigamond.
somerville: Somerville, just northwest of Boston and north of Cambridge, is the most densely populated municipality in New England.
southborough: Southborough includes the villages of Cordaville, Fayville and Southville, and part of the town is covered by the Sudbury Reservoir.
spencer: Spencer is a Worcester County town west of Worcester.
sterling: Sterling is a Worcester County town north of Worcester.
stoneham: Stoneham is about nine miles north of downtown Boston and is home to the Stone Zoo.
stoughton: Stoughton is about 17 miles from Boston and 31 miles from Providence.
sudbury: Sudbury is a MetroWest town with a long colonial history.
sutton: Sutton is a Blackstone Valley town designated a Preserve America community in 2004.
upton: Upton, first settled in 1728, is a Worcester County town southeast of Worcester.
uxbridge: Uxbridge, incorporated in 1727, calls itself the Heart of the Blackstone Valley and was an early textile center of the American Industrial Revolution.
waltham: Waltham was the original home of the Boston Manufacturing Company and a prototype 19th-century industrial city; today it is a center for research.
watertown: Watertown, one of the first Massachusetts Bay Colony settlements in 1630, is home to the Perkins School for the Blind.
wayland: Wayland was founded in 1638 as part of Sudbury and includes the village of Cochituate.
wellesley: Wellesley is home to Wellesley College, Babson College and a campus of Massachusetts Bay Community College.
westborough: Westborough, incorporated in 1717, is a Worcester County town governed by open town meeting.
westford: Westford is a Middlesex County town along Interstate 495, northwest of Boston.
weston: Weston, about 15 miles west of Boston, has one local historic district and ten National Register districts.
weymouth: Weymouth is the second-oldest settlement in Massachusetts, after Plymouth.
winchester: Winchester is a Middlesex County town about eight miles north of downtown Boston.
woburn: Woburn is a Middlesex County city about nine miles north of Boston.
worcester: Worcester is the principal city of Central Massachusetts and the second-most populous city in New England.
